claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
The multiple refractory elements in WTaTiVZr introduce local atomic-scale lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr lower the Peierls barrier or Peierls stress for dislocation motion.
The multielement chemistry and associated lattice distortions stabilize grain boundaries in WTaTiVZr.
A lower Peierls barrier enhances dislocation mobility in WTaTiVZr.
Enhanced dislocation mobility facilitates plastic deformation under high-temperature loading.
Stabilized grain boundaries and nanoscale heterogeneities blunt cracks and inhibit brittle crack propagation.
Relative to pure tungsten, WTaTiVZr should exhibit greater high-temperature plastic strain.
Relative to pure tungsten, WTaTiVZr should exhibit greater high-temperature fracture toughness.
Relative to pure tungsten, WTaTiVZr should exhibit delayed crack initiation under high-temperature mechanical loading.
Commercial pure tungsten has limited plasticity and lower toughness, leading to brittle behavior at high temperature.
At 1000–1200°C, thermally activated dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding are expected to dominate deformation in the tested regime.
Significant grain coarsening, oxidation, or radiation effects could independently alter the mechanical behavior and therefore fall outside the hypothesis's intended validity.
The role of lattice distortions in enhancing dislocation mobility is well established in some high-entropy alloys.
Powder metallurgy, hot isostatic pressing, and controlled annealing can produce a fine, stable grain structure in WTaTiVZr.
Matching the alloy and tungsten samples in grain size and impurity level controls those microstructural variables in the comparison.
Testing at 1100°C under identical inert-atmosphere conditions can compare tensile plasticity, creep behavior, fracture toughness, and post-mortem microstructure between WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten.
